paragraph:
Methods & Meanings
ABSOLUTE VALUE
Absolute value is the numerical value of a number without its sign. The symbol for absolute value is two vertical bars, | |, one on each side of the number. Absolute value can represent the distance on a number line between a number and 0. Since a distance is always positive, the absolute value is always either a positive value or 0. The absolute value of a number is never negative.
For example, the number −3 is 3 units away from 0, as shown on the number line. Therefore, the absolute value of −3 is 3. This is written |−3| = 3.
Likewise, the number 5 is 5 units away from 0. The absolute value of 5 is 5, written |5| = 5.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings
LETTERS IN MATHEMATICS
Letters are used in math in various ways, but they do not all represent the same thing. Here are five ways you may see letters used in this course.
1. Unknowns are letters that stand for a specific number that is not known yet. They are used in equations that are being solved.
For example, p is an unknown in the equation 3 + p = 5; p is a number that is not known yet, but it can be figured out.
2. Variables are letters that represent quantities that can change. They can take on different values while maintaining a particular relationship.
For example, x and y are variables in the equation 3 + x = y; as x changes, y changes, too.
3. Constants are letters that stand for fixed, unchanging values. They never vary within a problem or situation. Parameters are constants within specific problems or situations, but when parameters are letters, they can define a whole class of things, such as families of functions.
For example, the number π ≈ 3.14159… is a constant. π is a Greek letter used for the universal mathematical constant that represents the ratio of a circle’s circumference to its diameter. The value of π is always the same, no matter the circle.
Additionally, m and b are parameters in the equation y = mx + b; within a specific problem, m and b will have fixed values, such as −5 and 1, respectively, in y = −5x + 1. Yet, different values of m and b will yield different lines.
4. Labels are letters used as shortcuts for the purpose of naming or identifying. They do not represent a numerical value that changes or is solved for.
For example, f is a label in the equation f(x) = 2x + 3; the name of this function is f. (Note that this equation also has variables: x is the independent variable, and f(x), which represents the output of the function and is sometimes replaced with y, is the dependent variable.)
5. Placeholders are letters that represent values in general examples or rules. These are helpful when discussing properties that are true for a whole collection of values or when generalizing patterns.
For example, a is a placeholder in the property a^(−1) = 1/a; the letter a is used as a placeholder for any non-zero number.

paragraph: PROPERTIES OF REAL NUMBERS: The tile moves have mathematical names, called the properties of real numbers. Commutative Property: The order in which numbers or terms are added or multiplied is not important (e.g., a + b = b + a, a · b = b · a; non-examples: 7 - 2 ≠ 2 - 7, 50 ÷ 10 ≠ 10 ÷ 50). Associative Property: The grouping of numbers or terms being added or multiplied is not important (e.g., (a + b) + c = a + (b + c), (a · b) · c = a · (b · c); non-examples: (5 - 2) - 3 ≠ 5 - (2 - 3), (12 ÷ 4) ÷ 2 ≠ 12 ÷ (4 ÷ 2)). Identity Property of Addition: Adding zero to any expression gives the same expression (e.g., a + 0 = a; non-examples: 5a · 0 ≠ 5a). Identity Property of Multiplication: Multiplying any expression by one gives the same expression (e.g., 1 · a = a; non-examples: 6 + 1 ≠ 6). Additive Inverse Property: For every number a, there is an opposite number −a such that a + (−a) = 0. The sum of additive inverses is zero (e.g., 3 + (−3) = 0; non-examples: 8 − (−8) ≠ 0). Multiplicative Inverse Property: For every nonzero number a, there is a reciprocal number 1/a such that a · 1/a = 1. The product of multiplicative inverses is 1 (e.g., 6 · 1/6 = 1; non-examples: −3/5 + (−5/3) ≠ 1).

paragraph:
CONSTRUCT VIABLE ARGUMENTS AND CRITIQUE THE REASONING OF OTHERS

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings

INTERPRETING SLOPE AND y-INTERCEPT OF A LINEAR MODEL

A trend line and its equation provide a linear model that summarizes the association between two variables and enables you to make predictions. The slope of a linear model is the predicted change in the dependent variable (Δy) when the change in the independent variable (Δx) is 1 unit. When describing the slope of a linear model, always acknowledge that you are making a prediction, as opposed to knowing the actual value, by using words like "predict," "expect," or "estimate."

The y-intercept of a linear model is the predicted value of the dependent variable when the independent variable is zero. In statistical scatter plots, the vertical axis is not always drawn at the origin, so you may need to use the equation of the linear model to determine the y-intercept rather than looking at where the line crosses the vertical axis on the graph.

Also be careful about extrapolating the model too far—that is, making predictions that are far smaller or larger than the data values. Models can be valid within the range of the data, but the farther you go outside this range, the less reliable the predictions become.

When describing a linear association, you can use the slope, whether it is positive or negative, and its interpretation in context, to describe the direction of the association. For example, refer to the scatter plot of data about the weight of a car in thousands of pounds (x) and the fuel efficiency of the car in miles per gallon (y). The linear association is negative. The linear model shown has the equation y = 76 − 7.7x. The slope of −7.7 means that for every change in the weight by 1,000 pounds, the fuel efficiency is predicted to change by −7.7 miles per gallon.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings

RESIDUAL PLOTS

A residual plot is created in order to analyze the appropriateness of a linear model. A residual plot has an x-axis that is the same as the independent variable for the data. The y-axis of a residual plot is the residual for each point. Recall that residuals have the same units as the dependent variable of the data.

The residuals are calculated by subtracting the predicted values from the actual values. The form of the residual plot is then created using these differences, plotted using the same domain as the original scatter plot.

When a linear model is a poor fit, this is often evident in the residual plot. For example, if the actual association is curved, the data points will lie above the regression line for one section, below the line for another section, and then above again, or vice versa. This same curved pattern will appear in the residual plot. The residual plot reveals that the linear model is not the best model for the data.

Instead, the residual plot should show no clear pattern; the residual points should be randomly scattered around zero. This random scatter indicates that a linear model appropriately describes the form of the association.

paragraph:
NONLINEAR MODELS
For some data sets, a nonlinear model fits the data better and makes better predictions than a linear model. This can often be determined by comparing the residual plots of various models.
Sometimes the physical situation can provide clues about the type of model to use. When dealing with dry-ice sublimation, an exponential model makes physical sense because the quantity being measured decays over time.
A quadratic model would not have been very effective because of its U-shape, which implies that the process will reverse at some point. paragraph:
Methods & Meanings
EXPONENTIAL FUNCTIONS
An exponential function is a function of the form f(x) = ab^x where b > 0, b ≠ 1, and a ≠ 0. Note that the variable x is the exponent. All exponential functions of this form have the x-axis as an asymptote because f(x) ≠ 0.
The coefficient a is the y-intercept. For example, a = 3 for the function f(x) = 3 · 2^x. Therefore, in the table and graph of f(x) = 3 · 2^x shown, (0, 3) is the y-intercept.
The base b is the constant percent rate of change. For each additional unit of the x-value, the previous value of f(x) is multiplied by b. For example, in the table shown, the constant percent rate of change is 2.
For values of b > 1, the value of the function increases as x increases, and this is “exponential growth.” When 0 < b < 1, the value of the function decreases as x increases, and this is “exponential decay.”
A common application of exponential decay is half-life. Half-life is the amount of time it takes for half the original amount to remain. In problem 7-47, you saw that the half-life of uranium-235 is 704 million years. That is, it takes 704 million years until half the original amount of uranium-235 remains (no matter how much you started with).
Geometric sequences are a special case of exponential functions in which the domain is restricted to the positive integers.

paragraph: Methods & Meanings: THE QUADRATIC FORMULA. Why does x = (-b ± √(b^2 − 4ac)) / (2a) give the solutions of ax^2 + bx + c = 0? One way to derive this formula is to rewrite the standard form of a quadratic equation in a factorable form and solve for x. This process is shown. Begin with the quadratic equation in standard form, then multiply each side by 4a: ax^2 + bx + c = 0; 4a(ax^2 + bx + c) = (0)4a; 4a^2 x^2 + 4abx + 4ac = 0. Add b^2 − 4ac to each side to get a perfect square trinomial: 4a^2 x^2 + 4abx + b^2 = b^2 − 4ac. Factor the left side of the equation: (2ax + b)^2 = b^2 − 4ac. Take the square root of each side. Use absolute value to calculate the positive and negative values for 2ax + b, then solve for x: √( (2ax + b)^2 ) = √(b^2 − 4ac); |2ax + b| = √(b^2 − 4ac). 2ax + b = √(b^2 − 4ac) gives 2ax = −b + √(b^2 − 4ac), so x = (−b + √(b^2 − 4ac)) / (2a). −(2ax + b) = √(b^2 − 4ac) or 2ax + b = −√(b^2 − 4ac) gives 2ax = −b − √(b^2 − 4ac), so x = (−b − √(b^2 − 4ac)) / (2a). Finally, use the ± sign to write the formula as a single equation: x = (-b ± √(b^2 − 4ac)) / (2a). Notice that a cannot equal zero because you cannot divide by 0! However, if a = 0, then this equation would not be quadratic and you would not use this formula.

Methods & Meanings: INEQUALITY SYMBOLS
Just as the symbol “=” is used in mathematics to represent that two quantities are equal, the inequality symbols are used to describe the relationships between quantities that are not necessarily equal.

Symbol | Meaning in Words
< | Less than
≤ | Less than or equal to
> | Greater than

paragraph: METHODS & MEANINGS: SOLVING ONE-VARIABLE LINEAR INEQUALITIES. To solve a one-variable linear inequality, change the inequality to an equation and solve for x. The solution to the equation is the boundary point of the inequality. For example, x = 12 is the boundary point for the inequality 10 − 2(x − 3) ≥ −8, as shown: 10 − 2(x − 3) ≥ −8; 10 − 2(x − 3) = −8; 10 − 2x + 6 = −8; −2x + 16 = −8; −2x = −24; x = 12. Since the original inequality is true when x = 12, place your boundary point on the number line as a solid point. (When the inequality is < or >, the boundary point is not included in the answer and is indicated with an open circle at the boundary point.) Then test one value on either side of the boundary point in the original inequality to determine which set of numbers makes the inequality true. Testing x = 8: 10 − 2(8 − 3) ≥ −8 => 0 ≥ −8 (true). Testing x = 15: 10 − 2(15 − 3) ≥ −8 => −14 ≥ −8 (false). Since x = 8 produces a true statement, the region on the number line containing x = 8 is the solution, or x ≤ 12.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings: METHODS TO SOLVE SINGLE-VARIABLE EQUATIONS
Here are three different methods you can use to solve single-variable equations.

REWRITING
Use algebraic techniques to rewrite the equation. This often involves using the Distributive Property to eliminate parentheses. Then solve the equation using the solution methods you know.
Example:
  5(x - 1) = 15
  5x - 5 = 15
  5x = 20
  x = 4

LOOKING INSIDE
Choose a part of the equation that includes the variable and is grouped together by parentheses or another symbol. Make sure it includes all occurrences of the variable. Ask yourself, "What must this part of the equation equal to make the equation true?" Use that information to write and solve a new, equivalent equation that you can solve in fewer steps.
Example:
  5(x - 1) = 15
  5(?) = 15
  ? = 3
  (x - 1) = 3
  x = 4

UNDOING
Start by undoing the last operation performed on the variable. This will give you an equivalent equation that can be solved in fewer steps, which you can solve either by undoing the process again or with another approach.
Example:
  5(x - 1) = 15
  5(x - 1)/5 = 15/5
  x - 1 = 3
  x = 4

Examples

1. A bag of coins contains only nickels and dimes. If there are 33 coins and the total value is $2.40, how many of each kind of coin are in the bag?

SOLUTION
This problem can be solved using a single variable. Let d = the number of dimes. The number of nickels can be represented by the expression 33 – d. The value of dimes and nickels is then 10d and 5(33 – d), respectively. The total value of the dimes and nickels is 240 cents, so:

10d + 5(33 – d) = 240

Solving yields d = 15 dimes and 33 – 15 = 18 nickels.

A system of equations can also be written to solve this problem. Let d = the number of dimes and n = the number of nickels. Write an equation that relates to the number of coins, and a second equation that relates to the value of the coins.

d + n = 33
10d + 5n = 240

Solving this system yields d = 15 dimes and n = 18 nickels.

Methods & Meanings: SOLVING A QUADRATIC EQUATION
So far in this course, you have learned three algebraic methods to solve a quadratic equation of the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0. Each of the following examples demonstrates one of the methods.

EXAMPLE 1: Solve 3x^2 + x − 14 = 0 for x using factoring and the Zero Product Property.
First, make sure the quadratic expression is equal to 0. Then, factor the quadratic so it is written as a product: (3x + 7)(x − 2) = 0.
The Zero Product Property states that if the product of two terms is 0, then at least one of the factors must be 0. Thus, 3x + 7 = 0 or x − 2 = 0. Solving each equation for x reveals that x = -7/3 or x = 2. This method only works when the quadratic can be factored.

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings
EQUATIONS FOR SEQUENCES
ARITHMETIC SEQUENCES
The equation for an arithmetic sequence is f(n) = mn + b, where n is the term number, m is the sequence generator (the common difference), and b is the zeroth term. Compare these equations to a continuous linear function f(x) = mx + b, where m is the growth (slope) and b is the starting value (y-intercept).
For example, the arithmetic sequence 4, 7, 10, 13, … could be represented by f(n) = 3n + 1. (Note that “4” is the first term of this sequence, so “1” is the zeroth term.)
Another way to write the equation of an arithmetic sequence is to use the first term in the equation, as in f(n) = m(n − 1) + f(1), where f(1) is the first term. The sequence in the example could be represented by f(n) = 3(n − 1) + 4.
You could even write an equation using any other term in the sequence. The equation using the fourth term in the example would be f(n) = 3(n − 4) + 13.
GEOMETRIC SEQUENCES
The equation for a geometric sequence is f(n) = ab^n, where n is the term number, b is the sequence generator (the multiplier or common ratio), and a is the zeroth term. Compare these equations to a continuous exponential function f(x) = ab^x, where b is the growth (multiplier) and a is the starting value (y-intercept).
For example, the geometric sequence 6, 18, 54, … could be represented by f(n) = 2 · 3^n.
You can write a first-term form of the equation for a geometric sequence as well: f(n) = f(1) · b^(n − 1). For example, the first-term form would be f(n) = 6 · 3^(n − 1).

paragraph:
Methods & Meanings: GRAPHS WITH ASYMPTOTES

A mathematically clear and complete definition of an asymptote requires some ideas from Calculus, but some examples of graphs with asymptotes might help you recognize them when they occur. In the examples provided, the dotted lines are the asymptotes. In the two lowest graphs, the vertical axis, x = 0, is also an asymptote.

Asymptotes can be diagonal lines or even curves. In this course, asymptotes will almost always be horizontal or vertical lines. The graph of a function has a horizontal asymptote if, as you trace along the graph out to the left or right (that is, as you choose x-coordinates farther and farther away from zero, either toward infinity or toward negative infinity), the distance between the graph of the function and the asymptote gets closer to zero.

A graph has a vertical asymptote if, as you choose values of x closer and closer to a certain value, from either the left or right (or both), f(x) gets farther away from zero, either toward infinity or toward negative infinity.
